extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, media critics, and researchers interested in The New York Times controversies and journalistic standards
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the evaluative criteria and ethics repeatedly invoked in criticism of a major newspaper (The New York Times), covering accuracy, sourcing, editorial processes, balance, and harm-minimization. Useful for assessing journalistic practice and controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic phrasing should clearly specify the nature of alleged misconduct rather than using vague language (e.g., Tom Rosenstiel: "The phrasing is just too vague.").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe alleged behavior precisely and distinguish between fact, allegation, and speculation. Avoid ambiguous terms like "inappropriate" without explanation or examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reporting suppositions of anonymous aides about private sexual behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not report the suppositions or concerns of anonymous aides about whether a boss is "getting into the wrong bed." (Clark Hoyt: "I think it is wrong to report the suppositions or concerns of anonymous aides...").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from publishing unverified innuendo from unnamed sources about private sexual matters; if published, clearly label as unverified and weigh public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual accuracy and correction practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure factual accuracy; when errors occur, publish clear corrections listing the mistakes (example: Times printed a correction listing eight factual errors in a Walter Cronkite tribute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain strong fact-checking before publication; issue prompt, specific corrections when inaccuracies are discovered and explain the nature of each error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify visual and audiovisual evidence before asserting actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm whether an action is visible in footage before claiming it occurred (example: allegation that Geraldo Rivera "nudged" a rescue worker was later acknowledged as not visible on tape).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check video and audio evidence and avoid definitive claims about visible actions unless supported by the footage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve accurate context of quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not recontextualize or alter the meaning of interview quotes (M.I.A. article admitted to recontextualization of two quotes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish verbatim quotes where possible; if editing for length or clarity, ensure the edits do not change intended meaning and disclose significant edits or paraphrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and pushback in coverage of sensitive crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Present alternative views and push back on malicious or victim-blaming remarks rather than presenting them uncritically (Cleveland rape case criticized for failing to present an alternative view and for not pushing back).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting on allegations or community reactions, include context, alternative perspectives, and challenge harmful narratives (e.g., victim-blaming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid language that implies victim provocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid reporting details or phrasing that suggest victims 'provoked' assaults (criticized use of victim's clothing to imply provocation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about including descriptions that can be interpreted as assigning blame to victims; provide context and avoid unnecessary, potentially prejudicial details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantiate broad or systemic claims with robust evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting widespread practices (e.g., illegally low wages in an industry), back claims with clear, representative evidence; moderate language where evidence is not definitive (nail salon series controversy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document sampling methods, cite primary sources, and avoid overstating conclusions; be prepared to publish follow-ups and re-examinations if criticisms arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult subject-matter experts for sweeping historical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For large historical narratives, consult specialist historians and respect basic factual standards (1619 Project criticisms and admission of failing to consult experts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek external review by qualified historians for interpretive historical claims; correct overstated or unsupported assertions promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider law-enforcement and investigative harm before publishing leaked materials or photos
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid publishing leaked photos or documents that could undermine investigations or harm victims (Manchester bombing photos said to have 'undermined' police investigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance public interest against potential harm to investigations and victims; consult authorities when publication could compromise safety or evidence, and redact or withhold material as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify criminal admissions and corroborate claims before presenting them as fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of criminal acts (e.g., admissions on a podcast) must be independently verified; failure to verify can lead to retractions and loss of award consideration (Caliphate podcast couldn't verify and was withdrawn as a Pulitzer finalist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corroborate confessions or criminal claims with independent evidence and multiple sources before reporting them as factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vet op-eds for accuracy, context, and potential harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion pieces should meet editorial standards for vetting and context; failure can publish misinformation or encouragement of violence (Tom Cotton op-ed controversy: "failed to meet its editorial standards" and was described as "rushed").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply rigorous fact-checking and contextual review to op-eds, especially when they argue for extreme actions; ensure they do not advocate violence or spread demonstrably false claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain editorial roles (copy editors) to protect quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Dedicated copy editors check style, grammar, factual correctness, tone, and write headlines; eliminating these roles can increase typos and factual errors (elimination of copy editors criticized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve specialized editing roles or ensure their functions are effectively covered if roles are consolidated; prioritize final-read checks for accuracy and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid producing false balance and ensure commitment to objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present opposing views as equivalent when evidence strongly favors one side; avoid false balance in political stories (The Verge criticized the Times for presenting false balance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight sources and claims based on evidence; make distinctions between fact and opinion, and avoid framing contentious but unsupported claims as balanced parity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate labeling and careful use of descriptors to avoid defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use descriptors like "far-right misinformation site" carefully and correct labeling errors promptly (The Babylon Bee labeling dispute led to amendment and clarification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm characterizations with evidence; when labels are disputed, correct and clarify the record to avoid defamatory implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical handling and disclosure of anonymous or protected sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide carefully whether to withhold a source's name and how to describe their background and potential biases (Columbia applications hack intermediary was anonymized and described variably; Times criticized for muted description).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When withholding identity, explain why and provide as much contextual information as possible about the source's perspective or motives without revealing identity; be transparent about verification steps taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh newsworthiness and consistency when publishing hacked data
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance public interest against harm and precedent when publishing information obtained through hacking; be consistent in policy application (Times criticized for publishing hacked Columbia data after declining other hacked info).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a clear policy for handling illicitly obtained material, documenting why publication serves public interest and assessing potential legal/ethical harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond constructively to criticism with transparent follow-up reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When widespread criticism arises, re-examine reporting, publish follow-up stories, and acknowledge where language or findings should be toned down (public editor recommended follow-ups for the nail salon series).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat criticism as an opportunity for further investigation; publish updates, corrections, and context openly rather than defensive responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dismissive or mocking tone in candidate coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage should not focus unduly on a candidate's age, appearance, or style to the detriment of substantive reporting (2016 primaries criticism: tone was "regrettably dismissive, even mocking").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center reporting on policy positions and relevant performance; avoid ad hominem framing and superficial character critiques that distract from substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize legal standards in defamation reporting about public figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that public figures face a higher bar (actual malice) in libel suits and that litigation privileges may apply (Baldoni lawsuit dismissed; judge cited litigation privilege and public figure standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While aiming for accuracy, be mindful of legal thresholds and document verification steps for potentially defamatory claims about public figures; preserve records of reporting and fact-checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider national security and public safety implications of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether publication could be a "grave threat to our national security" or otherwise impede safety or investigations (publication of Manchester photos drew international condemnation and claims it threatened investigations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult security and law-enforcement stakeholders as appropriate, and weigh the urgency of public interest against potential risks to safety or investigations.
